newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FOCUS-Hang Seng shatters 12,000, others in Asia mixed.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Hang Seng shatters 12,000, others in Asia mixed.

text.p: Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index leapt ahead on Thursday to close above the key technical level of 12,000 for the first time in more than two and a half years, spurred by record overseas gains and good fundamentals at home.
The Hang Seng Index hit 12,004.33 shortly after the opening, soaring above the 12,000 mark for the first time since February 4, 1994, when it hit a high of 12,186.80.
The market then fell below Wednesday's close before rallying to end 62.68 points, or 0.52 percent, higher at 12,014.56.

"The market seems to be very strong particularly today. I think it is due to overseas markets..." said Edwin Cheung, dealing director at Taiwan Securities. "Corporate earnings are contributing to this rally."
"I expect to see the market continue to move ahead on the back of new highs in foreign markets...," said Anthony Mak, sales director at Vickers Ballas.
London and New York markets have set new highs as they reap the benefits of the current steady U.S. interest rate policy.

On Wednesday, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 29.07 points to 5,933.97, surpassing the previous record of 5,905 set on Tuesday. The Dow only pierced 5,900 on Tuesday and dealers were placing wagers on when it would hit 6,000.
In London, the FTSE 100 broke the 4,000 level for the first time to set a record for the second straight day.
The FTSE 100 ended at 4,015.1, up 22.9 points.

Elsewhere in Asia, Tokyo shares gave up early gains won on the back of Wall Street's advance, reflecting in part uncertainty over the outcome of the October 20 general election in the absence of any other factors.
The Nikkei 225-share index closed down 167.10 points, or 0.78 percent, at 21,331.50.
"The Dow's rise propped up the market for a while, but... there were few factors giving direction," a trader said.

Shares of companies with heavy exports, such as Honda Motor Co Ltd, advanced aided by a fall in the yen against the dollar. The U.S. currency hit a 32-month high of 112 yen before falling to 111.64 in late trade.
At 1045 GMT, the dollar had eased further still, trading at 111.38/1.48 yen and 1.5324/34 marks.
Taiwan stocks rallied after the government decided not to raise the business income tax. The weighted index ended up 73.34 points, or 1.12 percent, at 6,611.58.
Thai stocks remained pressured by political and local economic concerns, closing down 32.14 points or 3.04 percent at 1026.54.

Malaysian shares gained 8.40 points, or 0.74 percent, to close at 1,147.72 and Indonesia shares closed slightly up on speculative buying. The Jakarta Composite Index ended 0.48 points, or 0.08 percent, higher at 589.790.
Singapore traders ignored Wall Street's gains. The Straits Times Industrials Index closed down 12.13 points, or 0.56 percent, at 2,150.76.
In the Philippines, stocks lost 41.62 points, or 1.31 percent, to close at 3,130.26 as foreign fund managers moved their investments elsewhere.
Australia's All Ordinaries Index closed up 0.3 points, or 0.01 percent, at 2,314.56, while New Zealand shares gained 14.38 points, or 0.65 percent, to close at 2,235.73.

SIMEX Brent futures prices were traded lower in late afternoon dealings testing support around $23.00 per barrel. November last traded at $23.00, down 10 cents from London's settlement on Wednesday of $23.10.
Hong Kong's bullion market saw healthy two-way professional business before ending down from New York's close on Wednesday.
Bullion ended at US$379.40/379.90 an ounce against New York's US$379.75/380.25 close on Friday.
